newsitem.title: GERMANY: Ruehe says Bonn will go ahead with Eurofighter.
newsitem.headline: Ruehe says Bonn will go ahead with Eurofighter.

text.p: German Defence Minister Volker Ruehe said on Sunday he was confident Bonn, under pressure to tighten budgets and qualify for European monetary union, would find the funds needed to buy 180 Eurofighter jets to modernise the air force.

The minister said in a statement he welcomed proposals by Finance Minister Theo Waigel to redirect state aid for the Airbus airliner to the four-nation Eurofighter project to help toward the planned 23 billion mark ($13.6 billion) purchase.

Ruehe has already offered to provide a billion marks from his own budget, which was severely scaled back last year, if Waigel comes up with another billion needed to assure that production of the jet can start.

After months of delay dogged the project developed jointly by Germany, Britain, Italy and Spain, Waigel's proposals came as the latest sign the German finance ministry would at a pinch come up with the cash.
The government has said it badly needs the Eurofighters to replace the German air force fleet of ageing Phantom jets and it wants them in service by early next century.
Ruehe said he had bargained down the price by almost 30 percent in negotiations with industry and the only thing that remained to be done now was to secure the financing.

"We must get the financing right. I can't present a project to parliament worth 20 billion marks over 20 years unless it has a solid financial basis. This (financing) is basically possible," Ruehe said.

"Last November we reached a coalition agreement under which the finance minister said he would give me extra funds towards my budget for the jet. I would in turn be ready to scratch together a contribution for the project too," Ruehe said.
Ruehe said Waigel's proposal backed this previous pledge.

Daimler-Benz Aerospace AG (DASA), the German partner in the project, has said it was ready to discuss Waigel's proposal to use state aid granted to DASA for developing its Airbus business to the Eurofighter.

DASA said it was paying a million marks a day into its Eurofighter operations without the guarantee of a firm order from the German government. The aircraft's development has already cost the German taxpayer eight billion marks.
It is also being developed by Italy's Alenia SpA, Britain's British Aerospace Plc and Spain's state-owned CASA.
Partners Britain and Spain have committed to buying the Eurofighter, and Italy's parliament is reviewing procurement.
But the Bonn government has yet to place an order for the 180 Eurofighters.
A government decision on financing is expected in the next few weeks as part of drafting the 1998 budget. ($ = 1.693 German Marks)
